subject: Pause Now, Hike Later?

 Good morning! Here's the latest in trending: 

 Stellar results:  SK Hynix ( SKHY ) posts record profits , $75B shareholder return plan.

 Negotiating table: Trump administration discusses U.S. oil firms' return to Russia.

 Latest vote: Israeli markets respond as post-election coalition path remains unclear .  

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Top News
 
 
 
 FOMC watch 
 
 
 
Getty Images
 
 
The Federal Open Market Committee is widely expected to hold the federal funds rate target range at 3.75%-4.00% this afternoon. But that doesn't mean its job is done. Inflation remains well above its 2% goal, and September's 25-basis-point hike isn't likely to bring it down on its own.

 Zoom in:  With  inflation still dogging the Federal Reserve, does it make sense to hold? "Yes," Navy Federal Credit Union Chief Economist Heather Long said in an interview with Seeking Alpha. "The Fed likes to say it's not political, but hiking within a week of an election is a pretty bold political statement." A hike would also imply a sense of urgency "that there's something urgently wrong with the economy that needs to be addressed," Long  said. But whether the FOMC needs to increase its benchmark rate this month is a coin toss. "It's okay to wait a few more weeks and hike in December," Long  added. The risk profile hasn't changed much. And the data provided in the interim will give the policymakers a better sense of how broad-based the inflation problem is. According to the CME FedWatch tool, the probability of a 25-basis-point hike in December currently stands at 76.5%.  

 Looking ahead: Long expects the Fed will have more work to do in 2027. She's penciling in two more rate hikes , which is one more than the Fed policymakers signaled in their September Summary of Economic Projections. "It's going to take more effort to control inflation," she said. Once they're done hiking, it will take time for the higher rates to work their way through the economy. "My view is when they're done hiking, they're going to have to stay at that high rate for a lot longer than most people want," Long said. "So, I don't think we'll be talking about cuts until 2028, unless there's a recession." Reasons for holding rates that high for that long include high gasoline and diesel prices from the ongoing Iran war, inflation pressures from the AI boom, swelling medical costs and pressure building in the housing market.

 SA commentary: "I think higher yields are one of the main reasons why the Fed can afford to wait one more meeting, despite inflation running above 3% ," SA analyst Cain Lee stated, pointing to Treasury yields sitting above 5%. "The September jobs report gave the Fed a reason to wait, and the CPI gave it a reason not to wait past December," he added. The challenge for Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is no longer simply deciding whether inflation warrants another rate hike , SA analyst James Picerno said. "It is explaining how a decision to leave rates unchanged remains consistent with his repeated commitment to restoring inflation to the Fed’s 2% target," Picerno  added. "If policymakers stand pat while inflation risks continue to build, investors may conclude that policy tightening is merely being postponed rather than avoided, potentially fueling renewed upward pressure on Treasury yields."
